title: Library lending system
prompt: Design borrowing and returning physical book copies. Model a title separately from a lendable copy, and prevent one copy from being lent twice.
clarifyingQuestions: Are loans per physical copy or title?
Can a member hold multiple loans?
Are reservations and fines required?
functionalRequirements: Find available copies of a title
Return a copy and close its active loan
nonFunctionalRequirements: A copy has at most one active loan
Borrow and return must have atomic state transitions
Reject invalid state transitions without partial changes
outOfScope: Multi-region active-active writes in the baseline
Unspecified payment, billing or social features beyond the stated requirements
apiContracts: POST /copies/{id}/loans accepts memberId and returns loanId
POST /loans/{id}/return closes a loan idempotently
dataModel: BookCopy(id, titleId, state). Loan(id, copyId, memberId, borrowedAt, returnedAt). A database partial uniqueness constraint or equivalent transactional design enforces one active loan per copy.
mermaidDiagrams:
flowchart LR
 Member --> LendingService
 LendingService --> CopyRepository
 LendingService --> LoanRepository
 LendingService --> EligibilityPolicy
baselineDesign: Separate catalog metadata from copy availability. A lending service validates member eligibility and performs an atomic available-to-loaned transition before creating the loan. Return addresses a specific loan, so retrying an old return cannot close a newer loan for the same copy. Keep policy decisions, such as loan duration, behind a small interface only when they have real variation. Do not put mutable availability on a shared BookTitle object: several physical copies can be in different states. In a persistent implementation, lock or conditionally update the copy row and insert the loan in one transaction. An audit record captures who initiated the transition without becoming the source of current availability.
tradeoffs: A synchronized in-memory repository is easy to demonstrate but only coordinates one process
A database unique constraint is a stronger final guard than a prior availability query
Separate title and copy models add one join but preserve correct identity
failureModes: A borrower retries after a timeout
Two members request the last available copy
A return references a loan that is already closed
scalingOptions: Index title lookup independently from active loans
Partition high-volume audit events without weakening the active-loan constraint
concurrencyConcerns: An in-memory monitor protects the demo map
production borrowing and loan insertion need a shared transaction
Lock copies in a stable order if a request borrows several
testingStrategy: Test duplicate borrowing and unauthorized returns
Test two borrowers racing for one copy
Test retrying return after a new loan has started
followupQuestions: Which single invariant would you protect first?
How does a retry differ from a new logical request?
What happens after a timeout with an unknown outcome?
Which metric reveals the next bottleneck?
How would you recover after a process or storage failure?
Which requirement would force a different partitioning strategy?

These are self-assessment anchors, not company hiring cutoffs.

title: Vending machine state model
prompt: Design a machine that accepts credit and dispenses one selected product. Separate payment state from stock state and define what a failed dispense means.
clarifyingQuestions: Which payment instruments are accepted?
Can the customer cancel before dispensing?
Must change be exact?
nonFunctionalRequirements: Never dispense without enough credit
Never allow stock to become negative
Make a hardware failure visible for reconciliation
outOfScope: Multi-region active-active writes in the baseline
Unspecified payment, billing or social features beyond the stated requirements
apiContracts: insertCredit(amount) validates positive minor units
buy(slotId) returns a receipt or typed failure
cancel() returns outstanding credit
dataModel: Slot(id, productId, priceMinor, stock). MachineSession(id, creditMinor, state). DispenseAttempt(id, slotId, reservationId, hardwareOutcome). Store money as integer minor units.
mermaidDiagrams:
stateDiagram-v2

 Accepting --> Selecting: credit inserted
 Selecting --> Dispensing: stock reserved
 Selecting --> Accepting: cancel
 Dispensing --> Accepting: confirmed outcome
baselineDesign: Use explicit states for accepting credit, awaiting selection and dispensing. The state controls which commands are legal, rather than spreading boolean checks through every method. On selection, validate credit and stock together, reserve the item, then request hardware dispense. A real device can time out after actually delivering the product, so do not blindly repeat a hardware action. Record a unique dispense attempt and reconcile ambiguous outcomes. The runnable skeleton below deliberately models only an atomic in-memory purchase. It does not pretend to control physical hardware or implement a payment network. A richer hardware adapter should return confirmed success, confirmed failure or unknown outcome.
tradeoffs: An enum-driven state machine is simpler than one class per state for a small transition set
Reservation reduces overselling but requires expiry and reconciliation
Rejecting unsupported change is safer than silently retaining customer credit
failureModes: Power fails during dispense
A stock sensor disagrees with the inventory count
Payment succeeds but dispense confirmation is lost
scalingOptions: Keep hardware control local to each machine
Upload append-only reconciliation events to central operations
concurrencyConcerns: Stock and credit change inside one lock
External hardware effects require attempt identity and reconciliation
Concurrent cancellations cannot refund credit already committed to a purchase
testingStrategy: Test exact price and insufficient credit
Test the last item purchased by two callers
Inject confirmed failure and ambiguous dispense outcomes

title: Bounded LRU cache
prompt: Implement a fixed-capacity cache with least-recently-used eviction. Define whether reads change recency and how concurrent access is coordinated.
clarifyingQuestions: Is capacity measured in entries or bytes?
Are null keys and values legal?
Do updates count as access?
functionalRequirements: Get a value and promote its recency
Evict the least recently used entry when capacity is exceeded
nonFunctionalRequirements: Capacity is positive and never exceeded after an operation
Recency updates and eviction are atomic
Cache misses are distinguishable from stored values
outOfScope: Multi-region active-active writes in the baseline
Unspecified payment, billing or social features beyond the stated requirements
apiContracts: get(key) returns Optional value
put(key,value) updates recency and evicts when needed
dataModel: A hash index maps keys to nodes. A doubly linked list orders nodes from most to least recent. A LinkedHashMap in access-order mode combines these structures for a compact Java implementation.
mermaidDiagrams:
flowchart LR
 Caller --> CacheLock
 CacheLock --> HashIndex
 HashIndex --> RecencyList
 RecencyList --> Eviction
baselineDesign: Use one authoritative ordering representation; maintaining both a separate timestamp map and a linked list invites inconsistency. In the Java skeleton, LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true updates ordering on get, and removeEldestEntry enforces entry capacity after insertion. A synchronized boundary protects both reads and writes because reads mutate recency. This implementation is appropriate for a small in-process cache, not a distributed store. Adding TTL changes semantics: an expired key must not count as a valid hit, and a separate cleanup policy must prevent expired entries from consuming the whole capacity. Weight-based capacity requires tracking entry weights and deciding what to do with an entry larger than the entire limit.
tradeoffs: One lock is easy to reason about but limits concurrent throughput
Sharding reduces contention but yields per-shard rather than global LRU
Entry-count capacity ignores differing value sizes
failureModes: A hot key is removed by an incorrect recency update
A caller mutates a cached value
A single oversized value dominates memory
scalingOptions: Shard only after measuring contention
Prefer immutable values
Track hit ratio and load latency rather than only cache size
concurrencyConcerns: Access-order get is a write to the recency structure
Protect the map and list with the same synchronization protocol
A concurrent map alone cannot protect a separate eviction list
testingStrategy: Test recency on reads and overwrites
Test capacity one and invalid capacity
Compare randomized operation sequences with a simple reference model

title: Token-bucket rate limiter
prompt: Design a deterministic token bucket with explicit burst capacity and refill rate. Keep time injectable so boundary tests do not need real sleeps.
clarifyingQuestions: What is the burst allowance?
Is the limit per identity or global?
What happens when limiter storage is unavailable?
nonFunctionalRequirements: Tokens stay between zero and capacity
Refill and consumption are one atomic operation
Elapsed time cannot move the refill clock backward
outOfScope: Multi-region active-active writes in the baseline
Unspecified payment, billing or social features beyond the stated requirements
apiContracts: allow(nowNanos) returns an allow or reject decision
A service adapter maps rejection to HTTP 429 and a documented retry hint
dataModel: Bucket(capacity, refillPerSecond, tokens, lastRefillNanos). Use one monotonic time domain within a process. Shared storage needs its own authoritative timing policy.
mermaidDiagrams:
flowchart LR
 Request --> IdentityKey
 IdentityKey --> BucketLock
 BucketLock --> Refill
 Refill --> Consume
 Consume --> Decision
baselineDesign: At each request, compute elapsed duration since the previous refill and add elapsed times refillRate, capped by capacity. Update the refill timestamp, then consume a token if at least one exists. The lock protects the entire calculation. An injected monotonic timestamp makes tests precise and avoids wall-clock adjustments. The single-process model below intentionally rejects time regression. A real multi-instance limiter cannot simply keep one bucket in every instance while claiming a global limit: it needs shared atomic state, a partitioned authority or an explicitly approximate policy. Protect the identity map against unbounded growth with expiry and bounded key cardinality.
tradeoffs: Token buckets allow explicit bursts while smoothing average rate
Floating-point tokens are simple but integer fixed-point accounting gives tighter precision control
Global coordination improves accuracy but increases latency and failure coupling
failureModes: Time regresses or comes from inconsistent sources
Limiter keys grow without bound
Shared storage is unavailable during an attack
scalingOptions: Assign each key to one authoritative partition
Expire inactive keys
Measure rejection rate and backend saturation together
concurrencyConcerns: Refill and consume under the same lock
Do not combine timestamps from different machines
A distributed check-and-update needs an atomic storage operation
testingStrategy: Test initial burst and exact refill boundary
Test a long idle period caps at capacity
Test simultaneous callers and regressing time

title: URL shortener
prompt: Design creating short links and redirecting users. Focus on key uniqueness, read latency, abuse handling and durability.
clarifyingQuestions: Are custom aliases supported?
Can links expire or be edited?
What traffic and geographic reach should be assumed?
functionalRequirements: Report link-not-found separately from temporary storage failure
nonFunctionalRequirements: Redirect p95 target 100 ms within the serving region, an interview assumption
Committed links survive process restart
Enforce rate limits and destination validation
outOfScope: Multi-region active-active writes in the baseline
Unspecified payment, billing or social features beyond the stated requirements
apiContracts: POST /links accepts destination and optional alias with idempotency key
GET /{key} returns 302 with Location
DELETE /links/{id} requires ownership
dataModel: Link(key primary key, destination, ownerId, createdAt, expiresAt, state). Index ownerId and creation time for management. A unique key constraint is the collision authority.
mermaidDiagrams:
flowchart LR
 Client --> Edge
 Edge --> RedirectAPI
 RedirectAPI --> Cache
 RedirectAPI --> LinkDB
 RedirectAPI --> EventQueue
 EventQueue --> Analytics
baselineDesign: Start with a stateless API, a durable relational key-value-shaped table and an optional cache on the redirect path. Generate a random opaque key and retry collisions through a unique insert. The redirect reads the key, verifies active state and expiry, then returns a nonpermanent redirect when edits or abuse takedowns must propagate. The application must not fetch arbitrary destinations merely to redirect: server-side preview fetching introduces SSRF risk and requires a separate restricted fetcher. Cache popular links with a TTL matching the takedown requirement. Negative caching needs a short lifetime so newly created links do not remain invisible. Track aggregate redirect metrics asynchronously rather than making analytics writes part of every redirect transaction.
tradeoffs: Random keys distribute writes but need collision detection
Sequential identifiers simplify allocation but reveal activity and need an encoding strategy
Aggressive CDN caching improves latency but delays revocation
failureModes: A generated alias collides
Cache contains a disabled destination
The analytics pipeline is unavailable while redirects remain healthy
scalingOptions: Add read replicas only with an explicit freshness policy
Partition by key hash when one database no longer serves measured load
Use CDN caching selectively for immutable links

For this system, refine read/write ratio, retention, payload size and hot-key distribution before choosing infrastructure. Object bytes and chat bodies can dominate metadata; notification provider throughput and checkout inventory contention can dominate request count.

Cache invalidation races with redirect reads
Idempotency prevents duplicate creates after a timeout
testingStrategy: Test collision retries with controlled key generation
Test expiry and revocation while cached
Load test a hot key and a cold-cache restart

title: Checkout, inventory & payment
prompt: Design order checkout that avoids overselling and duplicate charges while handling ambiguous provider responses.
clarifyingQuestions: Are carts reserved before payment?
Which inventory consistency guarantees are required?
Is a payment authorization separate from capture?
nonFunctionalRequirements: Never treat a frontend price as authoritative
Deduplicate checkout and payment operations
Preserve an auditable order state
Release expired reservations safely
outOfScope: Multi-region active-active writes in the baseline
Unspecified payment, billing or social features beyond the stated requirements
apiContracts: POST /checkouts accepts cart reference and idempotency key
GET /orders/{id} returns authoritative state
POST /payment-webhooks verifies provider signature and records outcome
dataModel: Order(id, ownerId, currency, totalMinor, state, version). OrderLine(orderId, sku, quantity, priceMinor). Reservation(id, sku, quantity, expiresAt, state). PaymentIntent(id, orderId, providerReference, state).
mermaidDiagrams:
flowchart LR
 Client --> CheckoutAPI
 CheckoutAPI --> OrderDB
 CheckoutAPI --> InventoryAuthority
 CheckoutAPI --> PaymentProvider
 PaymentProvider --> VerifiedWebhook
 VerifiedWebhook --> OrderStateMachine
 OrderStateMachine --> Outbox
 Outbox --> Fulfillment
baselineDesign: Create an immutable priced order snapshot on the server using current catalog rules. Reserve inventory with a conditional decrement or a reservation ledger under a transaction. Record the payment intent before contacting the provider, then use the provider's idempotency contract. A timeout leaves an unknown outcome, not a safe-to-retry-new-charge outcome. Verified webhooks and reconciliation queries drive idempotent state transitions. Confirm the order only when the required payment state is established. A saga coordinates reservation expiry and payment compensation because a database transaction cannot span an external provider. Keep an audit trail of transitions and make operators able to reconcile stuck states without manually rewriting balances.
tradeoffs: Holding stock during payment reduces overselling but temporarily lowers availability
Authorization then capture can reduce refunds but depends on provider capability
Strong consistency for stock may increase latency during a hot sale
failureModes: Payment succeeds after reservation expiry
A webhook is duplicated or delayed
A reservation release races with order confirmation
scalingOptions: Partition inventory authority by SKU
Serialize hot-SKU reservation updates
Queue noncritical notifications and analytics outside checkout
capacityEstimation: Illustrative assumptions, not measured demand: 1 million operations per day is approximately 11.6 requests per second on average. At a 20× peak, budget for roughly 232 requests per second. At 1 KB metadata per operation, raw metadata grows about 1 GB per day before indexes and replicas. For this system, refine read/write ratio, retention, payload size and hot-key distribution before choosing infrastructure. Object bytes and chat bodies can dominate metadata; notification provider throughput and checkout inventory contention can dominate request count.
concurrencyConcerns: Use version checks on order transitions
Reservation expiry must compare current state and ownership
Payment and inventory retries must carry stable logical operation IDs
testingStrategy: Simulate provider timeout after successful authorization
Race reservation expiry with payment confirmation
Replay webhooks and verify no duplicate fulfillment
followupQuestions: Which single invariant would you protect first?
How does a retry differ from a new logical request?
What happens after a timeout with an unknown outcome?
Which metric reveals the next bottleneck?
How would you recover after a process or storage failure?
Which requirement would force a different partitioning strategy?
evaluationRubric: Score requirements, invariants, baseline correctness, failure recovery and tradeoff explanation from 1 to 5. A 1 names components without a coherent flow; a 3 provides a consistent baseline and handles the main failure path; a 5 ties concurrency, recovery, security and measured capacity to explicit requirements. These are self-assessment anchors, not company hiring cutoffs.
